intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that multiple epiphyseal dysplasia-2 (EDM2) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the COL9A2 gene (120260) on chromosome 1p34.2.

paragraphs.text: Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia (MED) is a dominantly inherited chondrodysplasia characterized by mild short stature and early-onset osteoarthrosis; some forms clinically resemble mild pseudoachondroplasia (Briggs et al., 1994). EDM2 is a form of MED caused by mutation in the gene encoding the alpha-2 chain of type IX collagen, and has been described as a subtype in which the hips are not markedly affected at an early age (Fiedler et al., 2002).

paragraphs.text: Versteylen et al. (1988) described 2 families that appeared to contain examples of multiple epiphyseal dysplasia. In both families there was a striking incidence of severe osteochondritis dissecans of the knees. The authors suggested that the osteochondritis was caused by the fragmented and maldeveloped epiphyses characteristic of epiphyseal dysplasia.

paragraphs.text: Fiedler et al. (2002) reported a family of 19 individuals over 4 generations in which 12 members were affected with a variant of multiple epiphyseal dysplasia in which the hips were not markedly affected at an early age. Beginning in childhood, the disease led to pain and stiffness of the knees, ankles, elbows, and finger joints. Some adult patients repeatedly suffered from free articular bodies resulting in locking of the joint, and affected individuals were prone to the development of early degenerative joint disease.

Using a single-strand conformational polymorphism within the murine Col9a2 gene, they mapped that gene to mouse chromosome 4.

paragraphs.text: In a 4-generation family with EDM2, Fiedler et al. (2002) screened candidate regions and identified a G-to-C substitution at position -1 in the exon 3/intron 3 splicing region of the COL9A2 gene, which they predicted most probably alters splicing. The substitution was confirmed in 8 clinically affected family members and in 3 presymptomatic young children. Screening was performed by automated sequencing and BsaWI digestion of amplicons. Fiedler et al. (2002) concluded that, together with previous reports, mutations leading to skipping of exon 3 within the COL3 domain of the alpha-2 chain of collagen type IX may be relatively common in patients with this MED subtype in which the hips are not markedly affected at an early age.

paragraphs.text: In affected members of a 4-generation family with EDM2, Fiedler et al. (2002) identified a G-to-C substitution at position -1 in the exon 3/intron 3 splicing region of the COL9A2 gene, which they predicted most probably alters splicing. The family had 12 affected members, with childhood onset of pain and stiffness of the knees, ankles, elbows, and finger joints, free articular bodies with joint locking in some adults, and early degenerative joint disease; the hips were not markedly affected at an early age. The substitution was confirmed in 8 clinically affected family members and in 3 presymptomatic young children.
